prompt.context: Our client is a Private Equity fund that has made a number of acquisitions in the past few years, mainly in the pulp, paper and packaging industries. Our client just made a recent acquisition of Packaging Inc., a large US-based packaging company, in the hope of driving synergies with one of the fund's existing portfolio companies, Aluminum Inc. One of the main areas where our client thinks they can achieve synergies is in the companies' supply chains.
prompt.question: Do you agree with this assumption and if so, what synergies do you think are possible and how would you quantify the potential benefits?

clarifying_info.q: What products does Packaging Inc. sell and to whom?
clarifying_info.a: Packaging Inc. sells food packaging containers (mainly made out of foam) to Retail customers (e.g. Wal-Mart type stores) and to Restaurant customers, mainly via large distributors.

clarifying_info.q: What products does Aluminum Inc. sell and to whom?
clarifying_info.a: Aluminum Inc. sells aluminum packaging products to Retail and Restaurant customers.

clarifying_info.q: Are there any differences in the physical characteristics of each company's products?
clarifying_info.a: Packaging's products are very light but take up lots of room. Aluminum's products are dense — heavy but take up little room.

clarifying_info.q: Is there seasonality in either business?
clarifying_info.a: Packaging Inc. has a peak in the summer. Aluminum Inc. has a peak around Thanksgiving.

clarifying_info.q: How should we define the supply chain?
clarifying_info.a: Assume 'supply chain' can be defined from the procurement of raw materials all the way to the final delivery of finished products.

clarifying_info.q: Should we consider operations outside the US?
clarifying_info.a: No, ignore operations outside of the US.

clarifying_info.q: Can I see a map of the two companies' current footprint?

exhibits.title: Current Footprints
exhibits.shows: A US map showing the locations of manufacturing plants, Packaging Inc. warehouses, and Aluminum Inc. warehouses, accompanied by a table breaking down facility counts and total square footage by customer type (Restaurants, Retail, Both) for each company.

exhibits.title: Total Freight Expenses by Mode ($m)
exhibits.shows: A bar chart showing freight expenses broken down by mode (Truckload, Less Than Truckload, Intermodal, Small Package) for Packaging Inc., Aluminum Inc., and a combined total.

exhibits.title: Post-Integration Freight Assumptions
exhibits.shows: A table of cost per pound per mile by mode for each company, plus a list of mode-shift assumptions that will apply after integration.

integration_assumptions: Either company can benefit from optimal rates
50% of previous Less Than Truckload shipments can now go Truckload
25% of previous Truckload shipments can now go Intermodal
30% of previous Small Package shipments can now go Less Than Truckload
Total miles and total pounds shipped do not change

framework: Better Understand the 2 Companies: baseline supply chain costs; understand each company's business, customers, strengths/weaknesses
Potential Synergies — Procurement: raw materials (bulk buying, fewer suppliers); services (transportation, warehousing labor); other (machines, repair parts)
Potential Synergies — Manufacturing: number of plants; utilization of lines; shared expertise/techniques

Potential Synergies — Transportation: inbound from raw material sources (minor — different inputs); outbound to customers (major — same customers, complementary load characteristics); optimized truck loads (foam is volume-constrained, aluminum is weight-constrained — mixing improves utilization)
Potential Synergies — Warehousing: consolidate footprints to reduce fixed costs; reduce overall labor through economies of scale
Potential Synergies — Inventory: less seasonality impact (summer peak vs. Thanksgiving peak offsets); fewer holding locations after facility consolidation
Quantifying Potential Benefits: use benchmarks; build data models; compare existing contracts

questions.prompt: Question 1: Look at Exhibit 1. What do you learn about the two companies and the potential synergy opportunities from this map?
questions.guidance: Strong answers note: (1) Packaging Inc. has far more sites (36 vs. 11) and far more square footage (15.9m vs. 1.0m); (2) most plants and warehouses are co-located geographically; (3) heavy footprints in California, Chicago, and the eastern seaboard — near large metro areas; (4) Packaging Inc. has many combined Retail/Restaurant facilities while Aluminum Inc. has none; (5) Packaging Inc. has very few dedicated Retail facilities but those are very large; (6) Aluminum Inc.'s facilities are much smaller on average. Opportunity implications: Aluminum Inc. can leverage Packaging's broader network to reach more regions and cut long-distance freight costs for heavy products; consolidate overlapping facilities (e.g. southern CA); combine Retail/Restaurant into shared locations; rationalize very small and very large (>800k ft²) facilities toward an optimal size.

questions.prompt: Question 2: Given Exhibits 2 and 3, what freight savings can you estimate by combining the two companies?
questions.guidance: Two-step calculation: (Step 1) Apply rate optimization — every shipment uses the lower of the two companies' per-unit rates. (Step 2) Apply mode optimization — shift volume to cheaper modes per the assumptions. Candidate should recognize the before total is $183m and work toward a new total of $158.25m, yielding savings of $24.75m (approximately 13.5%).

math.setup: Starting combined freight = $183m. Step 1 — compute mode volumes after mode shift (using Packaging Inc. volumes because they are larger/drive the shift math shown in the casebook). Step 2 — apply post-integration rates to new volumes.
steps: Mode shift — Truckload: Packaging 92 (unchanged) + Aluminum 24 reduced by 33% ≈ 16 = 108 → round to 116 before rate step; after rate step 87 + (1-25%)×29 = 87 + 21.75 = 108.75
Mode shift — LTL: Packaging 4 (unchanged) + Aluminum 10 (unchanged) = 14 → after rate step 7 + (1-50%)×7 = 7 + 3.5 = 10.5
Mode shift — Intermodal: 26 + 3 = 29 (unchanged in rate step) = 29
Mode shift — Small Package: Packaging 2 reduced by 33% ≈ 1.34 + Aluminum 8 = ~10 → unchanged in rate step = 10
math.answer: $24.75m savings per year, approximately 13.5% reduction in total freight costs

recommendation: Significant synergies exist in the combined supply chain across procurement, manufacturing, freight, warehousing, and inventory
Freight savings alone are estimated at $24.75m per year (13.5% of combined freight spend)
risks: Freight savings assumptions may be too aggressive — actual rate sharing and mode optimization may be limited by contractual, operational, or regulatory constraints
Freight is only one supply chain area; we do not yet know whether other areas will yield comparable savings
Integration efforts are complex and can cause significant operational disruptions during execution
next_steps: Investigate all other supply chain opportunity areas (procurement, manufacturing, warehousing, inventory) and prioritize by savings potential
Assess capital requirements for each initiative and calculate NPVs
Begin implementation with the highest-NPV projects first
